posts.title: Dear Atheist, If God Exists, Why Is He So Hidden?
posts.content:
Dear Atheist,

Suppose you wanted someone to know you existed.

You could make your presence unmistakable. You could reveal yourself to every person on earth in a way that left no room for confusion. Every nation would know. Every language would have a name for you. No one would have to wonder whether you were real.

If you were also perfectly loving and desired a relationship with humanity, why would you remain hidden?

I can see why this question troubles you.

The world contains people who have never believed in God, people who once believed and gradually lost their faith, and people who have spent years searching for Him without reaching the certainty they hoped for.

Some have prayed with tears in their eyes. Others have studied the Bible, examined religious claims, and asked questions they were afraid to voice in church. Some have watched suffering unfold and wondered how a loving God could remain invisible through it all.

Then some seem to encounter God with remarkable certainty. They speak of answered prayers, divine encounters, and a presence they cannot easily explain to someone who has never experienced it.

Why does the same world appear so full of God to some people and so silent to others?

Philosophers call this problem divine hiddenness. The philosopher J. L. Schellenberg developed an influential argument that a perfectly loving God would remain open to a relationship with every capable person. If someone is sincerely open to God and still cannot believe that He exists, what explains that person’s inability to find Him?

I think this deserves more than a quick answer.

What Would Count as God Making Himself Known?

When we ask why God is hidden, we should first examine what we expect revelation to look like.

Perhaps we imagine God appearing in the sky, speaking audibly to every human being, or providing evidence so overwhelming that disbelief becomes impossible. That would settle one question for many people: whether some powerful supernatural being exists.

Other questions would remain.

Would everyone who witnessed such a revelation understand who God is? Would they trust Him? Would they love Him? Would they willingly submit their lives to Him?

Knowledge of someone’s existence and knowledge of their character are different experiences. You can know that a person exists without understanding them, and you can understand many things about someone while remaining unwilling to trust them.

This distinction matters to Christian theology because the Christian claim is that God desires more than recognition of His existence. He desires to be known.

Yet I want to be careful here. Human relationships also depend on access, communication and presence.

If someone consistently hides from you, their desire for a relationship becomes difficult to understand.

Telling the person who cannot find you to search harder does not resolve the problem. The same difficulty applies to divine hiddenness. If God desires a relationship with humanity, why do some sincere seekers experience His absence so deeply?

The Christian Claim Is That God Has Revealed Himself

Christianity does not begin with the idea of a God who has said nothing about Himself.

Its central claim is that God has acted within history and made Himself known through revelation, culminating in the person of Jesus Christ. Hebrews 1:1–2 describes God as having spoken through the prophets in the past and, in these last days, through His Son. John 1:18 presents the Son as the one who has made the Father known.

The Christian understanding of revelation is therefore personal and historical. It points to the life of Jesus, His teachings, His death and the resurrection that Christians believe followed. This gives us something concrete to examine. The question becomes whether the historical claims about Jesus provide sufficient reason to believe that God has revealed Himself.

A person may examine the available historical evidence and reach a different conclusion from a Christian. That disagreement deserves serious engagement. Simply repeating that God has revealed Himself does not establish that every person has adequate grounds to recognise that revelation.

There is another question worth sitting with, though.

Could God have made Himself known in ways that are less obvious than we expect?

Christianity points to Scripture, creation, conscience, the person of Jesus and the work of the Holy Spirit. Romans 1:20 presents creation as bearing witness to God’s invisible attributes. Acts 17:27 describes humanity as seeking God, with the possibility of reaching out and finding Him, since He is not far from each one of us.

These passages express the biblical conviction that God has made Himself knowable. They also raise questions about interpretation. Nature can inspire wonder, yet people disagree about what the universe reveals about its origin. Conscience can direct us toward moral questions, yet people disagree about the source of morality. Religious experiences can transform lives, yet people from different traditions interpret similar experiences through different beliefs. The existence of these experiences does not settle every dispute about God. It does give us something worth investigating.

Does Unmistakable Evidence Leave Room for Freedom?

One response to divine hiddenness is that God may wish for human beings to seek Him freely.

If God appeared in a way that made His existence impossible to deny, perhaps people would obey out of fear, submit out of self-preservation or follow religious practices because the consequences of refusing seemed unbearable.

A relationship shaped by love seems to require some freedom.

Still, this explanation has limits.

We know that other people exist. We know that our parents, friends and colleagues exist. That knowledge does not force us to love them. We can acknowledge someone’s existence while resisting their influence, disliking their character or refusing their requests. In the same way, knowing that God exists would not automatically produce love for God.

The Bible itself portrays people who encounter extraordinary manifestations of divine power and continue to resist Him. Pharaoh witnesses the signs described in Exodus and still hardens his heart. The Israelites witness God’s acts during the exodus and later struggle with distrust and disobedience. These accounts suggest that awareness of God’s power and a willing relationship with Him are separate matters.

But the atheist can reasonably ask why God could not provide clearer evidence while still leaving people free to respond as they choose. I do not think the appeal to human freedom completely answers that question. It offers one possible consideration within a wider Christian understanding of God, though it leaves open why the evidence available to sincere seekers differs so significantly across different people and circumstances.

Perhaps we should resist claiming more certainty about God’s reasons than Scripture actually gives us.

What About the Person Who Sincerely Searches and Finds Silence?

This is the part of the question I find most difficult to dismiss.

It is easy to speak about seeking God when you believe you have found Him. It is harder to explain His hiddenness to someone who has spent years searching and feels that every attempt has led nowhere.

Psalm 13 begins with David asking, “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?”

Those words are in the Bible.

The Psalms preserve the prayers of people who feel abandoned, confused, and distant from God. Scripture gives room to lament. It records the anguish of Job, the questions of the prophets and the cry of Jesus on the cross: “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

This matters because biblical faith does not require us to pretend that God’s presence is always easy to perceive. There are seasons when prayer feels effortless and seasons when words seem to fall into silence. There are times when Scripture comes alive with meaning and times when familiar passages feel distant. A person can continue to believe while wrestling honestly with the experience of God’s apparent absence.

For the believer reading this, I hope that distinction brings some comfort. The feeling that God is absent is an experience worth acknowledging. It does not, by itself, establish that He has abandoned you.

For the atheist, these biblical passages may not establish that God exists. They do reveal something about the faith being examined. The Christian tradition has preserved the voices of people who struggled to understand God’s actions and sometimes questioned His apparent silence. That honesty deserves to be taken seriously.

Is God’s Hiddenness Evidence Against His Existence?

It can be part of a serious argument against belief in God.

If a perfectly loving God desires a relationship with every person, and some people remain sincerely open to such a relationship while finding no adequate reason to believe, the situation requires an explanation. A Christian may respond by examining the nature of revelation, the effects of human limitations, the possibility of divine encounters that are not immediately recognised and the broader claims of Scripture. An atheist may conclude that the distribution of religious belief and disbelief fits a world without a God who desires universal relationship.

Both positions involve judgments about what the available evidence means.

I find it helpful to separate two questions here. First, has God provided sufficient evidence for His existence? Second, if God exists, why has He chosen to reveal Himself in the ways Christianity describes? An answer to one does not automatically settle the other.

And perhaps this is where the conversation becomes more meaningful. Rather than treating doubt as a defect that must be corrected, we can examine what the doubt is actually asking us to understand.

A Final Thought

Dear Atheist, I cannot promise that every sincere search for God will end with an experience you “recognise” as His presence. I cannot give you a simple explanation for every unanswered prayer or every person who has struggled to believe.

I can tell you what Christianity asks us to consider.

It asks us to look at Jesus and examine the claim that God has made Himself known through Him. It asks us to consider the testimony of Scripture and the history of the Christian faith. It invites us to seek understanding, even when our questions remain difficult. And it leaves us with the image of a God who, according to Acts 17:27, is not far from each one of us.

Perhaps you find that claim unconvincing. Perhaps you are unsure what to make of it. Perhaps you have been asking this question for years. I would rather you examine it honestly than pretend to believe something you cannot yet accept.

And to the believer who has quietly wondered why God feels so distant, I hope you know that your questions have a place in the story of faith.

You can bring them to God without disguising their weight.

The question of divine hiddenness would forever remain open for serious examination.

I think it invites us to think carefully about evidence, love, freedom, and the kind of relationship God desires with humanity.

If God exists and desires to be known, what would you reasonably expect that relationship to look like?

I think that is a question worth carrying with us.

~ TEA

posts.title: Dear Atheist, Why Would a Good God Allow So Much Evil?
posts.content:
Dear Atheist,

Suppose you walked into a room and found a child dying of a disease she had no way of understanding.

Suppose her parents had prayed, pleaded, and exhausted every resource they had, yet she still died.

What would you say about God?

Perhaps you would ask why an all-powerful God watched it happen. Perhaps you would wonder what kind of goodness permits such suffering when stopping it should be within His power.

I think that is a fair question.

In fact, I think it is one of the strongest objections to Christianity.

The problem of evil has troubled philosophers for centuries. It has challenged the faith of believers, shaped the arguments of atheists, and forced Christian thinkers to examine what they mean when they call God good.

I want to take the question seriously.

Or rather, in epistemic and moral humility, let me attempt this question.

Because when we talk about evil, we are talking about things that happen to actual human beings. People lose their children. Families are destroyed by war. Someone is abused by a person they trusted. A young man dies before he has had the chance to live the life he imagined.

These experiences deserve more than a quick theological explanation.

So let’s begin with the question itself.

If God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and perfectly good, why does He allow so much evil?

The Argument Is Stronger Than Many Christians Admit

The classical problem of evil can be expressed through a few related claims.

If God is all-powerful, He has the ability to prevent evil. If God is all-knowing, He is aware of every instance of suffering and its consequences. If God is perfectly good, He would be opposed to evil. Yet evil exists, and some of its consequences are devastating.

There are two versions of the argument worth separating.

The logical problem of evil asks whether God’s existence is logically incompatible with the existence of evil at all. The evidential problem of evil asks something harder: whether the amount, intensity, and apparently pointless distribution of suffering makes God’s existence less likely even if not logically impossible.

That distinction matters.

A Christian might argue that God and evil are logically compatible. The atheist can then press a more difficult question: why would a good God permit this particular world, with this concentration of suffering? That version of the argument is harder to dismiss, and I want to sit rather than deflect.

What Do We Mean by Evil?

Before asking why God permits evil, it is worth examining what we mean when we call something evil.

When someone says they dislike suffering, they are describing a preference. When someone says it is wrong to torture an innocent child for pleasure, they are making a moral claim that appears to reach beyond personal taste. They are saying something about the act itself.

That raises a philosophical question worth naming early: what makes evil objectively wrong?

Christianity grounds moral reality in the character of God. Human beings possess dignity because they are made in God’s image, and moral goodness connects to who God is by nature.

This gives the Christian a basis for saying that cruelty is wrong even when a society approves of it, or when a powerful person benefits from it.

There is something else worth noticing inside the problem of evil itself.

When we object to suffering, we usually believe that something has gone wrong with the way reality ought to be. We look at abuse and think a person should never have been treated that way. We see injustice and believe the victim deserved better. That intuition, that human beings have a claim on how they ought to be treated, is one the Christian worldview takes seriously. It says that human dignity is grounded in something deeper than social agreement or personal preference.

That alone does not solve the problem. It does help explain why the Christian sees evil as a violation of the good God intended for creation, rather than simply an unpleasant feature of a morally neutral universe.

Human Freedom Explains Some Evil

Consider the terrible things people do to one another.

Genocide. Murder. Sexual abuse. Betrayal. Exploitation. Corruption. These are not merely unfortunate events. They involve human choices. A person decides to use power to dominate someone weaker. A leader chooses personal gain while people suffer. Someone entrusted with another person’s well-being chooses to cause harm instead.

The free-will defence argues that a world containing meaningful freedom may necessarily permit the possibility of people choosing evil. If God created beings capable of genuine moral choices, those choices carry consequences. Love, generosity and courage have meaning partly because they are chosen. Their opposites become possible for the same reason.

Of course, this raises a further question.

Could God have created beings who were free yet always chose what was right? Philosophers disagree about whether genuine freedom requires the ability to do otherwise, and the debate is serious. What the free-will defence cannot do is explain every form of suffering.

It helps us understand why God might permit destructive human choices. It leaves open the harder question of why He permits those choices to harm people who never consented to bear their consequences.

A child born into a war zone did not choose the war. A victim of abuse did not choose the abuser.

If anything, the Christian account makes responsibility heavier rather than lighter. People will answer for how they use the lives, power, and opportunities entrusted to them.

Human freedom is not an excuse. However, it is an explanation.

But What About Natural Evil?

This is where the argument becomes harder to answer quickly.

An earthquake does not make a moral decision. Cancer does not choose its victim. A child can be born with a painful condition through no fault of anyone in her family. A flood destroys a village. Someone dies in an accident despite taking every reasonable precaution.

Philosophers call these events natural evil, suffering that arises from natural processes rather than human choices. Free will does not immediately explain them.

Some Christian responses appeal to the regularity of the natural world. A universe with stable physical laws allows human beings to learn, plan, make decisions, and act meaningfully within it. Those same laws can produce earthquakes, disease and destructive weather.

A world with gravity allows us to walk, build and inhabit the earth. Gravity also makes falls possible. A world with biological processes allows life to develop and flourish. Those same processes involve deterioration and disease.

This line of thinking helps explain why a stable natural order might include risks. But the objection persists.

Could God have designed a natural order with fewer destructive consequences? Could He intervene more often without undermining the coherence of the world? The regularity argument explains why consistent physical laws might be a feature of a world God created for free moral beings. It does not establish that every instance of natural suffering is necessary, or that the present distribution is the best God could have arranged.

A thoughtful Christian should admit the limits of this response.

Does God Have to Prevent Every Evil?

There is another distinction worth examining before we move further.

Allowing something to occur is not the same as approving of it. A surgeon causes temporary pain while treating a condition. A parent may allow a child to face a difficult consequence in order to develop something important. These examples show that the presence of pain does not automatically mean an action is wrong.

But they also reveal the limits of the comparison.

A surgeon has a specific medical reason for the pain he causes. A parent can often explain, with some transparency, why a difficult experience was permitted. Human beings can examine those reasons and evaluate them. When we extend this reasoning to God, the scale changes entirely. What reason could justify the suffering of a child who dies in agony? What good could outweigh what certain people endure throughout their lives?

It would be intellectually dishonest to answer every such question by inventing a hidden divine purpose and calling it settled.

The Bible itself does not permit Christians to assign a specific reason to every tragedy. The book of Job is instructive here. Job’s friends repeatedly attempt to explain his suffering. They assume they understand what has happened and why. Much of their counsel is challenged by the narrative itself. Their certainty becomes part of the problem.

There is a lesson in that for anyone who wants to speak about suffering. We should be careful about claiming to know why God permitted a particular tragedy when we have no actual basis for that claim. Christianity makes a broad claim about God’s purposes in history. That is very different from pretending to have an explanation for every painful event we encounter.

The Christian Story Does Not Call Evil Good

One of the most important distinctions in Christian theology is the difference between God bringing good out of evil and God declaring evil to be good.

Consider Joseph in Genesis. His brothers betray him, and he suffers because of their deliberate actions. Years later he tells them:

“You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.”
Genesis 50:20

Notice what Joseph does not say. He does not say the betrayal was morally acceptable. He does not say his brothers acted rightly because the outcome eventually benefited others. Their intentions were evil. Their actions caused real harm. Yet those actions did not have the final word over Joseph’s life.

The Christian claim is that God can bring good out of events people intend for evil, working within a damaged world without turning wrongdoing into righteousness.

A person who survives abuse may develop a deep compassion that shapes the rest of their life. That does not make the abuse necessary or justify what the abuser did. Good can emerge in the aftermath of suffering while the suffering itself remains something to grieve, resist and, where possible, prevent.

Christian hope should never become a reason for passivity in the face of preventable harm.

Look at What Christianity Places at the Centre

Here is something I find remarkable about the Christian response to suffering.

At the centre of the Christian story is a man who suffers unjustly. Jesus is betrayed by someone close to Him. He is subjected to a corrupt process, mocked, beaten, and executed. Christians believe Jesus is God incarnate.

That means the Christian claim about God is not that He observes suffering from a comfortable distance. In Jesus, God enters human history and experiences human vulnerability.

The cross does not provide a neat explanation for every tragedy. It does something different. It reveals what Christians believe God is willing to endure to redeem humanity.

Then comes the resurrection.

The resurrection matters because Christianity does not present suffering and death as the final state of reality. It claims that God has acted within history and will ultimately overcome death itself. Paul writes:

“The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.”
1 Corinthians 15:26

Notice the word enemy. Death is not celebrated or accepted as an ideal feature of existence. It is something Christianity expects God to defeat. God does not merely ask humanity to accept suffering as an unchangeable condition. The Christian story points toward the restoration of creation, not simply the management of its brokenness.

What About the People Who Never Receive Justice?

Some people spend their entire lives suffering. Some are abused and never see their abusers held to account. Some die without receiving an apology, without seeing any consequence for the harm done to them.

If death is the final state of personal existence, some wrongs appear to remain permanently unresolved.

Christianity makes a claim about this. It teaches that there will be a final judgment and a restoration of creation. Human actions carry weight beyond the limits of this life. Victims are not forgotten, and perpetrators do not ultimately escape moral accountability because they avoided earthly justice.

Revelation describes a future in which God addresses what this world left unfinished:

“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore.”
Revelation 21:4

This is a promise about the future, not an explanation that removes the pain of the present. A person grieving today still grieves. A person facing injustice still needs protection and advocacy now. The hope of restoration gives Christians a reason to believe that suffering will not have the final word. It does not make present suffering insignificant, and it does not give anyone a reason to delay seeking justice while they are still alive to pursue it.

The credibility of this hope depends, of course, on whether the broader Christian account of reality is true, including its claims about Jesus and the resurrection. That is a separate argument, and it needs to stand on its own.

Does Evil Disprove God?

The logical problem of evil faces the challenge of showing that a perfectly good, all-powerful God could have no morally sufficient reason for permitting any evil whatsoever. If it is even possible that God has such a reason, the strict logical contradiction has not been established.

The evidential problem is harder.

The sheer amount of suffering in the world, particularly suffering that appears to produce no greater good, remains a serious challenge for Christian theism. A Christian needs to give an account of why a good God would permit a world that looks like this one.

I don’t think intellectual honesty requires pretending the problem has been solved beyond dispute. What I do think is worth recognising is that the existence of evil raises a difficult question about God without automatically settling every question about whether God exists. The two things are related, but they are not the same thing.

A Question Worth Returning

If there is no God, what should we make of the suffering that fills human history?

An atheist can believe suffering is bad, that human beings deserve compassion, and that we should work to reduce cruelty. Many atheists have developed thoughtful ethical frameworks for these convictions. The question is not whether an atheist can care about people.

The deeper question concerns the nature of moral reality itself. Are human beings valuable in an objective sense? Is there a moral truth about how we ought to treat one another? Christianity says that human beings have intrinsic worth because they bear God’s image.

That conviction places a responsibility on Christians. If we believe every human being carries God’s image, we should be among those most committed to protecting the vulnerable, confronting injustice and alleviating preventable suffering. A theology that explains evil while remaining indifferent to its victims has missed something central to the story it claims to believe.

Christians Should Not Be Afraid of This Question

Some treat questions about evil as evidence of weak faith. I think that is a mistake.

The Bible contains lament. The Psalms ask how long God will allow the wicked to prosper. Job demands an answer. The prophets cry out against injustice. Jesus weeps at the tomb of Lazarus.

There is space within the Christian tradition for grief, protest and questions that do not resolve quickly.

Faith does not require us to pretend that suffering is easy to understand. It asks us to consider what we believe about God in the presence of suffering, not to suppress the difficulty of the question but to bring it with us rather than leave it outside.

And here the Christian makes its central claim.

God is good. Human beings are responsible for much of the evil they inflict on one another. Creation is damaged by suffering and death. God has entered human history through Jesus Christ. Through the cross and resurrection, Christians believe God has begun the work of redemption that will culminate in the restoration of all things.

That account does not tell us why every tragedy happens. It offers a way of understanding evil as something God opposes and intends ultimately to overcome.

So, Dear Atheist...

I understand why suffering makes belief in God difficult.

I understand why a person who has watched someone they love suffer might struggle to reconcile that experience with the idea of a good and powerful God. I would never want to answer that pain with a clever argument and then walk away.

The Christian answer rests on several claims: that human freedom carries genuine moral responsibility, that a stable natural world can include suffering as a feature of its regularity, that God can bring good out of evil without endorsing it, that Jesus reveals God’s willingness to enter human suffering rather than observe it from outside, and that death and injustice will not have the final word.

You may disagree with those claims. You may find the suffering in this world too difficult to reconcile with them. That is a conversation worth continuing.

But consider one thing before we finish.

Christianity does not claim that the world as it currently stands represents the final expression of God’s purposes.

It claims that something has gone profoundly wrong with creation, that human beings participate in that brokenness, and that God has acted through Jesus Christ to redeem what has been damaged. The Christian hope is that God will judge evil, restore creation, and bring suffering to an end.

If Christianity is true, then the world we see today is real, and it matters, and it is not the whole story.

That is a claim worth examining carefully before dismissing it.

The problem of evil is the question I receive most often, and it is the one I take most seriously. The next letter in this series turns to the historical Jesus. Who was He? What can we actually know? And why does what we believe about Him matter more than most people realise?

Until then, keep thinking.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: Dear Atheist, Who Created God?
posts.content:
Dear Atheist,

I was waiting for this one.

It usually arrives early in the conversation, and it arrives with a certain confidence, as though it settles the matter once and for all.

“If God created the universe, then who created God?”

I understand the appeal. The argument seems to catch the theist in a trap. You say everything has a cause. The universe has a cause. God is that cause. Fine. But then, by your own reasoning, God must also have a cause. And whatever caused God must itself have a cause. And so on, infinitely. You have not explained the universe. You have just pushed the problem back one step.

It is a sharp objection.

But I think it rests on a misunderstanding of what the cosmological argument actually claims, and once we examine that misunderstanding carefully, the question changes shape entirely.

What the Cosmological Argument Actually Says

Let me be honest about something first.

The version of the cosmological argument that gets quoted in most conversations is not the version that philosophers actually defend.

“Everything has a cause, therefore God.”

That sentence is easy to attack, and it deserves to be attacked, because it is too simple to be useful.

If everything has a cause, then God has a cause too. The argument seems counterproductive.

But that is not the argument.

The serious versions of the cosmological argument make a more careful claim. They do not say everything has a cause. They say contingent things require explanation.

That distinction is very important.

Contingency and Necessity

A contingent thing is something that exists, but did not have to exist.

You are contingent. The specific combination of circumstances, decisions, biology, timing, and events that produced you could have gone differently. You could have never existed. But here you are. That is contingency. Your existence is real, but it is not necessary.

The question the cosmological argument raises is this: can we explain the existence of a contingent reality by appealing only to other contingent things?

Think about it carefully. If I ask why a particular book exists, you might say someone wrote it. If I ask why the writer exists, you trace back through parents, biology, evolution, the formation of the planet, the conditions of the early universe. Every step in that chain is contingent. Each thing could have been otherwise.

But if the entire chain is made up of contingent things, then the chain as a whole is contingent. And a chain of contingent things does not explain itself. You have told me what everything depends on.

You have not told me why there is something for everything to depend on in the first place.

At some point, the explanation has to terminate. Either it terminates in something that simply exists contingently with no further explanation, which is what philosophers sometimes call a brute fact, or it terminates in something whose existence is not contingent.

Something that could not have failed to exist. Something whose existence is necessary rather than accidental.

The cosmological argument proposes that the second option is more philosophically satisfying than the first.

So Who Created God?

Now we can return to your question.

The question assumes that God is a contingent thing. It assumes that God is the kind of entity that could have failed to exist, that God sits inside the same category as chairs, planets, and people, things that require a cause because they did not have to be here.

But that is precisely what the classical Christian doctrine of God denies.

Christianity does not say God is a very large or very powerful contingent being who happened to create everything else.

It says God is the one necessary being. The ground of existence rather than another piece of it.

The reason there is something rather than nothing, rather than just another something that needs explaining.

When someone asks, “Who created God?” they assume God is contingent. But if God is necessary, the question does not apply. You cannot ask what caused the thing whose existence is uncaused by definition.

Now, I can already hear the objection forming.

“That sounds like you are defining God into existence. You just decided God doesn’t need a cause. How convenient.”

That is fair pushback. Let me take it seriously.

Is This Just a Definitional Trick?

No. But I understand why it looks that way.

Here is the issue. The objection “who created God?” only carries force if every possible being is contingent.

If that premise is true, then yes, whatever produced the universe must itself have a producer, and you get an infinite regress with no explanation anywhere.

But the question is whether that premise is actually true. Is it the case that every possible being must be contingent?

That is not obvious. It is not even clearly true. The concept of a necessary being is not incoherent. Mathematics contains things that seem to exist necessarily. The truths of logic do not appear to be contingent. The number two did not come into existence at some point and might cease to exist tomorrow.

Its existence, if we grant that abstract objects exist at all, seems to have a different character from the existence of a chair.

Now, whether God exists is a separate question from whether the concept of necessary existence is coherent. But the cosmological argument is not trying to sneak God past you through a definitional loophole.

It is pointing out that the question “who created God?” presupposes something that needs to be argued for, not assumed.

If you want to say that everything requires a cause, you need to defend that claim carefully. Because the moment you grant that something might exist without a cause, you have opened the door to necessary existence. And then the question becomes not whether necessary existence is possible, but what that necessary being is like.

The Infinite Regress Problem

There is another way to approach this.

Suppose you reject the idea of necessary existence entirely. Suppose you say the universe simply exists, uncaused, as a brute fact, and there is no further explanation.

That is a coherent position. But notice what you have done.

You have accepted that something can exist without a cause. You have just located that thing differently. The theist says the uncaused thing is God. You say the uncaused thing is the universe, or the laws of physics, or some primordial quantum state, or whatever you believe preceded the observable universe.

At that point, both of you have accepted that something exists without a prior cause. The disagreement is about what that something is and what properties it has.

That is a much more interesting conversation than the original question suggested.

But What If the Universe Always Existed?

Some people try to escape the cosmological argument by proposing an eternal universe. If the universe has always existed, there was no beginning and therefore no need for a cause.

This is a serious proposal, and it deserves a serious response.

The first thing to note is that modern cosmology does not particularly favour it. The evidence we have, from the expansion of the universe to the cosmic microwave background, points toward a beginning. The standard model includes a singularity. None of that is philosophically conclusive, but it does suggest that “the universe is eternal” is not the default scientific position.

The second thing to note is that even an eternal universe does not dissolve the philosophical problem.

An eternal thing can still be contingent. If the universe could have been different, if the laws of physics could have taken other values, if there is no necessity in the universe’s particular character, then its eternity does not explain why it is the way it is. Eternity tells you how long something has existed. It does not tell you why it has the particular properties it has rather than some other properties, or rather than nothing at all.

The cosmological argument is not simply about beginnings. It is about contingency. And a contingent thing does not explain itself no matter how old it is.

God Is Not Another Object Inside the Universe

This brings us to something I think is genuinely important, and something Christians themselves sometimes fail to communicate clearly.

When people imagine God in these conversations, they often imagine a very large, very powerful person sitting somewhere outside the universe and deciding to create it. A kind of cosmic craftsman. A being among beings, just a significantly more impressive one.

That picture is not the classical Christian account of God.

The Christian tradition, working from Scripture and centuries of careful theological reflection, describes God as the one in whom all things live and move and have their being. Not a being inside existence, but the ground of existence itself. Not another item in the inventory of reality, but the reason there is an inventory at all.

Thomas Aquinas called God pure being. Not a being, but the act of existing itself, in which all other existence participates.

That is a radically different picture from the cosmic craftsman. And it means that the question “who made God?” is not just unanswered. It is the wrong question, in the same way that asking “what is north of the North Pole?” is the wrong question. The categories do not apply.

Now, you might think this classical doctrine of God sounds suspiciously abstract. You might prefer a God you can argue with directly. I understand that. But theological precision is not evasion. It is an attempt to think carefully about what God would have to be like in order to actually be the explanation for everything.

Why This Matters Beyond the Philosophy

These are not merely academic questions. They have texture. They press on something real.

When someone asks “who made God?”, there is often something underneath the question. A desire to understand. A suspicion that religion is filling in the gaps with an easy answer. A frustration with conversations that never seem to arrive anywhere definite.

I respect that.

I think the honest response is not to pretend the philosophy is easy. The cosmological argument does not hand us God on a silver platter with all properties specified. It takes us to the conclusion that a necessary, uncaused ground of existence is more philosophically coherent than an unexplained brute fact. It does not, by itself, tell us that this necessary being is personal, or good, or interested in human beings.

That is where Christian theology enters the conversation. The philosophical argument clears space. Christian claims about revelation, history, and the person of Jesus fill it. Those claims can be examined on their own terms. They should be examined on their own terms.

But the cosmological argument does something important before any of that. It establishes that the universe is the kind of thing that calls for explanation. It challenges the assumption that the default position is atheism and the burden lies entirely with the theist. It suggests that a necessary being is not a philosophical invention designed to dodge a difficult question, but a response to a genuine feature of reality.

Back to Your Question

Who created God?

The cosmological argument does not say God was created. It says God is the uncaused cause, the necessary being in whom contingent reality is grounded.

You can reject that conclusion. You can argue that necessary existence is incoherent, or that the universe itself is the better candidate for brute existence, or that the argument simply does not work. Those are real debates worth having.

But the question “who created God?” does not, by itself, defeat the argument. It assumes the argument makes a claim it does not make. And assumptions buried inside questions deserve to be brought out into the light and examined.

That is, after all, what we are here to do.

I know this raised more questions than it answered. That is intentional. These letters are not trying to settle centuries of philosophy in a few paragraphs. They are trying to demonstrate that the conversation is richer than it usually appears.

The next letter in this series takes up the problem of evil. If God exists and is good, why does the world look the way it does? It is the hardest question I have been asked, and I will not pretend it is easy.

Until then, keep thinking.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: Dear Atheist, Why Do You Believe There Is No God?
posts.content:
Dear Atheist,

Can I ask you a question?

Why do you believe there is no God?

I am not asking this sarcastically.

Well, perhaps there will be a little sarcasm along the way. You know me.

I am asking because I think this question deserves more attention than we usually give it.

When a Christian says, “I believe God exists,” the conversation often moves very quickly.

“Prove it.”

“Where is your evidence?”

“Why should I believe something I cannot see?”

“Religion is just faith.”

Fair enough. Those are legitimate questions. I actually think Christians should be able to answer them.

But there is another question sitting quietly underneath the conversation.

What exactly justifies the conclusion that God does not exist?

Let’s Begin With Something Important

Atheism is not one perfectly uniform position.

Some atheists mean, “I believe God does not exist.” Others mean, “I don’t have a belief in God.”

There is also agnosticism, which concerns whether we should suspend judgment about God’s existence entirely. That distinction matters.

If you say:

“I don’t believe in God because I haven’t encountered evidence that convinces me.”

I understand what you mean. You are describing your position.

If you say:

“There is no God.”

You have made a claim about reality. Those are different claims.

And claims about reality require reasons. Solid logical(not emotional) reasons./

The Difference Between Doubt and Disproof

Imagine I tell you that there is a particular species of fish living somewhere in the deepest parts of the Pacific Ocean.

You say: “I haven’t seen it.” Fair.

You say: “I’ve searched the places accessible to me and haven’t found it.” Also fair.

Then you say: “Therefore, that fish does not exist anywhere in the Pacific.”

Now you have moved beyond your evidence.

Your inability to find something is not automatically evidence that the thing does not exist. Sometimes it can be. Sometimes the thing in question would be so observable that its absence would count strongly against its existence.

That is precisely why the question of God’s existence is more complicated. God, by definition within classical Christianity, is not supposed to be an object somewhere inside the universe waiting to be discovered with a telescope.

He is understood as the transcendent creator and sustainer of the universe.

So when someone says:

“Where is God? Show me God.”

The Christian response cannot simply be, “Look harder.” We have to ask a prior question.

What kind of evidence would we reasonably expect if God existed?

That is where the real conversation begins.

“But You Have the Burden of Proof”

Yes.

If I say, “God exists,” I have a burden to give reasons for believing that. I am happy to carry it.

But there is an important philosophical distinction here. The fact that someone has given a reason for believing a proposition does not automatically make its negation the default truth.

Suppose I say:

“There is a reason the universe exists.”

You respond:

“I don’t see the reason.”

That doesn’t establish:

“There is no reason.”

It establishes that you have not accepted the proposed reason. Those are different conclusions.

The problem is that sometimes the atheist argument quietly moves from:

“You haven’t demonstrated God to my satisfaction.”

to:

“Therefore God does not exist.”

There is a missing step in the middle. And that step needs to be defended.

So What Reasons Are There for Believing in God?

This is where Christians sometimes make things unnecessarily difficult.

Someone asks for evidence for God and the Christian responds: “Because the Bible says so.”

That answer will probably not take us very far with someone who doesn’t already accept the Bible as divine revelation.

The Christian case can begin earlier. With reality itself.

Consider the fact that anything exists at all. You are here. I am here. The universe is here. Stars exist. Galaxies exist. Matter exists. Conscious beings exist.

There is something rather than nothing.

And the question is surprisingly stubborn:

Why is there something rather than nothing?

Science can tell us an enormous amount about how the universe behaves. It can investigate the early universe. It can describe physical processes. It can model cosmic development. Those achievements are extraordinary.

But the philosophical question remains:

Why does there exist a reality with physical laws, matter, energy, and an ordered structure capable of being described by mathematics in the first place?

That is where the cosmological arguments enter the discussion.

The Universe Is Not an Explanation of Itself

One family of philosophical arguments begins with contingency.

A contingent thing is something that exists but could have failed to exist. You and I are contingent. You did not have to exist. Your parents could have made different decisions. Different events could have occurred. You could have never been born.

The same basic intuition can be extended to the universe. Could the universe have been different? Could it have failed to exist? If yes, then we have a universe whose existence calls for explanation.

The argument is not:

“Everything has a cause, therefore God.”

That would immediately produce the obvious question: “Then who caused God?”

The more sophisticated argument is about the distinction between contingent and necessary existence. If everything that exists were contingent, then we would still have the question of why this entire contingent reality exists. The proposal is that there must ultimately be something whose existence is not dependent upon something else. A necessary reality. A reality that does not merely happen to exist.

The Christian identifies that ultimate reality as God.

Now, I know what you are thinking.

“Hold on, Ezra. You haven’t proved Christianity yet.”

Correct. And this is important. A cosmological argument, by itself, does not hand us the entire Christian doctrine. It is part of a cumulative case. The philosophical argument takes us toward an ultimate explanation. Christian theology then makes further claims about the nature of that ultimate reality.

That distinction matters because good reasoning should respect the distance between premises and conclusions.

“Why Can’t the Universe Just Exist?”

Good question.

It could be proposed. But notice what has happened. You have not solved the mystery. You have named the mystery.

“The universe just exists.”

That is a possible position. Philosophers sometimes call something like this a brute fact. The question becomes whether brute fact is the most satisfying explanation of reality. And now we are doing philosophy.

Because both positions have philosophical costs.

The theist says: “There is an ultimate necessary reality that explains why contingent reality exists.”

The atheist may say: “Reality simply exists without an ultimate explanation.”

The conversation therefore isn’t between someone who has an explanation and someone who has none. It is a disagreement about what kind of explanation reality requires.

That is a much more interesting conversation.

But What About Science?

This is where we need to slow down. Because I have heard this one many times.

“Science has explained the universe. We don’t need God anymore.”

My question is: Explained which part?

Science is extraordinarily powerful at describing physical reality. It investigates measurable phenomena. It constructs models. It tests hypotheses. It makes predictions. Those achievements are real and significant.

But saying that science explains physical processes does not automatically answer every metaphysical question.

If I explain how a computer operates, I have not answered every question about why the computer exists. If I explain how a sentence is grammatically structured, I have not explained why someone wrote the sentence. If I explain how stars form, I have not necessarily answered why there is a universe containing stars, laws and mathematical regularities capable of being studied in the first place.

Science and philosophy can therefore meet at the borders of their questions. The existence of scientific explanation does not automatically eliminate the philosophical question of ultimate explanation.

“But Maybe There Is Another Explanation”

Absolutely. There could be. And this is where Christians need intellectual humility.

The existence of alternative explanations means that we should examine them. That is how serious inquiry works. The question isn’t: “Can I imagine another possibility?” Of course you can.

The question is:

Which explanation best accounts for the totality of what we observe?

That brings us to something I find fascinating. The atheist is often asking the Christian to explain the world. I think the Christian should happily accept that challenge. Then I would gently return the question.

Can your worldview explain the things you are asking me to explain?

Where does the universe ultimately come from? Why does anything exist? Why is reality intelligible? Why does consciousness exist? Why do we experience moral obligations? Why do rational minds have the capacity to discover truths about reality? What explains the existence of persons who can sit here and ask questions about existence itself?

These questions don’t prove Christianity by themselves. But they make atheism far more philosophically interesting than the simple sentence:

“There is no evidence.”

There is evidence. The debate is about what that evidence means.

And Then There Is Consciousness

This one fascinates me.

You are not merely a collection of physical objects. You have subjective experience. You experience pain. You experience beauty. You think. You reason. You remember. You imagine. You can contemplate your own existence. You can ask whether your thoughts correspond to reality.

There is a profound philosophical problem here.

How does subjective conscious experience arise from purely physical processes?

There are physicalist accounts of consciousness, and the philosophy of mind contains serious arguments on multiple sides. I am not going to pretend one paragraph settles that debate.

But I will say this: consciousness is a philosophical problem for which “the brain does it” is not yet a complete philosophical explanation. The brain is obviously involved. The question is what that involvement ultimately means.

Then There Is Morality

You probably know where I am going.

“Without God, morality doesn’t exist.”

I think that sentence is too simplistic. Atheists can be deeply moral people. Atheists can sacrifice for others. They can love their children. They can oppose injustice. They can give generously. They can live remarkably disciplined lives.

The question is different.

What makes a moral obligation objectively binding?

There is a difference between:

“I don’t like murder.”

and

“Murder is objectively wrong.”

The first describes a preference. The second makes a claim about moral verity.

Perhaps objective morality exists independently of God. There are secular moral realist positions that attempt to defend precisely that. Again, the question deserves serious engagement.

But Christianity offers an explanation. Moral reality is grounded in the nature of God. Human beings possess dignity because they are made in God’s image. Moral obligations are ultimately connected to the character of the One whose nature defines goodness.

You can reject that explanation. But you have to provide an alternative account of what makes moral truths objectively true.

That is the conversation.

So, Do I Have a Mathematical Proof for God?

No. And I don’t think the Christian faith requires one.

We do not normally establish the most important conclusions in life through mathematical demonstration. You don’t mathematically prove that your mother loves you. You don’t mathematically prove that another person’s mind exists. You don’t mathematically prove that the external world exists independently of your perception.

You reason from evidence. You compare explanations. You consider coherence. You examine testimony. You assess explanatory power. You ask which worldview makes better sense of the reality we experience.

That is how much of human reasoning works. Christian belief can operate within that same intellectual space.

Faith Is Not the Same Thing as Believing Without Evidence

And let me address this quickly; this is one of the biggest misunderstandings I think Christians have allowed to develop.

“Faith” has sometimes been presented as: “Believe something even though there is no reason to believe it.”

That isn’t the Christian picture.

Hebrews 11:1 describes faith in terms of confidence concerning what is hoped for and conviction concerning what is unseen. Christian faith involves trust. Trust can be grounded in reasons.

If I tell you that I will meet you tomorrow and you trust me, your trust is based on something. You know me. You have experienced my character. You have heard my word. You have evidence from previous interactions. Trust goes beyond the evidence available at a particular moment, but it is not necessarily detached from evidence.

Christianity makes a similar move. The Christian does not claim to have placed God under a microscope. The Christian claims to have reasons for believing that God exists and that He has revealed Himself.

But Here Is Where I Think the Atheist Should Be Careful

You don’t have to believe in God. Seriously.

You are allowed to reject Christianity. You are allowed to think the arguments fail. You are allowed to remain unconvinced. You are even allowed to say:

“I have examined the arguments and I don’t think the evidence is sufficient.”

That is an intellectually respectable position.

But there is a difference between saying “I am unconvinced” and saying “There is no God.”

The first describes your response to the evidence. The second describes the structure of reality. The second requires considerably more confidence.

And this is where I want to return to the question I started with.

Dear Atheist, Why Do You Believe There Is No God?

If your answer is “Because I have never seen God” — I would ask whether you think every real thing must be directly visible.

If your answer is “Because science has not demonstrated God” — I would ask whether science is equipped to settle every metaphysical question.

If your answer is “Because there are bad things in the world” — I would want to talk about evil and divine goodness. We will. Very soon.

If your answer is “Because religion is psychologically comforting” — I would ask whether the psychological origin of a belief determines its truth or the absence of it.

If your answer is “Because there are many religions” — I would say: Good. Let’s compare their claims.

If your answer is “Because there is no evidence” — then I would invite you to examine the evidence before reaching that conclusion.

I Am Not Asking You to Believe

I am asking you to investigate. That also matters to me.

Because I think Christians sometimes make the conversation too easy for atheists. We give shallow answers. We quote a Bible verse when the person has asked a philosophical question. We tell someone to “just have faith” when they are asking about evidence. We become defensive when someone raises an objection. Then we wonder why the person remains unconvinced.

Christianity should be able to survive examination.

If God is real, honest investigation is not His enemy.

So, Dear Atheist, bring your questions. Bring the difficult ones. Bring the philosophical ones. Bring the scientific ones. Bring the historical ones. Bring the ones that Christians have been avoiding.

I intend to do the same.

Because I don’t think faith becomes stronger by refusing to think. I honestly think faith becomes more intellectually responsible when it is willing to meet serious questions in the open.

One Last Question

You asked me: “Why do you believe there is a God?”

Fair question.

My answer is that I find the existence of God to be the most coherent explanation of a reality that contains contingent existence, order, intelligibility, consciousness, moral experience and human rationality, alongside the historical claims Christianity makes about Jesus—which are very solid and reliable.

I don’t expect that sentence to settle the matter. It shouldn’t. A worldview this significant deserves more than a paragraph.

And that is exactly why I started this series.

So, Dear Atheist...

Let’s talk.

I have questions for you too.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: Christians are Delusional
posts.content:
Billions of Christians gather around the world every Sunday to pray to a God they cannot see.

Live a righteous life, or at least try to, to please a God they cannot see.

Christians are delusional.

At least, that is what some people think.

We organise our lives around a book written thousands of years ago. We restrain desires that we could indulge. We forgive people who hurt us. We give away things we could keep. We are told to love our enemies, care for the poor, pursue holiness, discipline our appetites and live with eternity in view.

From the outside, I can understand why someone might look at all of this and ask:

Why would anyone do this?

The usual explanations are familiar.

Maybe we are afraid of hell.

Maybe we were raised in Christian homes and inherited the belief system before we were old enough to question it.

Maybe we need God psychologically.

Maybe we are simply afraid of death and have constructed a comforting story around it.

These explanations are worth examining. I have no problem with examining them.

But I have a question of my own.

Suppose all of it were wrong.

Suppose one day we discovered that there is no God.

Suppose there is no final judgment.

Suppose there is no resurrection.

Suppose death really is the end.

What exactly would the Christian have lost by living this way?

The Hypothetical

Of course, there would be things.

A Christian might have abstained from certain pleasures that could have been enjoyed.

Perhaps they could have pursued sexual relationships without the boundaries Christianity imposed.

Perhaps they could have accumulated more money by being less generous.

Perhaps they could have taken revenge on people who hurt them.

Perhaps they could have lived with fewer restrictions.

But is that the most compelling alternative?

Imagine discovering at the end of your life that there was no God and no justice after death.

What would you suddenly wish you had done?

Would you wish you had been less forgiving?

Would you wish you had loved your family less faithfully?

Would you wish you had given less?

Would you wish you had been more consumed by greed?

Would you wish you had indulged every appetite simply because you could?

Would you wish you had become less disciplined?

I struggle to imagine that.

And this is where the argument becomes much more interesting to me.

Christianity Is Also About Becoming

Christianity does not merely promise something after death.

It proposes a particular way of becoming human before death.

It takes the development of the person seriously.

Your desires matter.

Your thoughts matter.

Your character matters.

Your treatment of other people matters.

Your relationship with money matters.

Your sexuality matters.

Your capacity for self-control matters.

Your response to suffering matters.

Your willingness to forgive matters.

Your concern for the vulnerable matters.

Even your private life matters when nobody is watching.

Christianity is profoundly interested in who you are becoming.

And perhaps this is one of the things we miss when we reduce religious belief to fear of hell.

A person who genuinely takes the Christian life seriously is being asked to become a particular kind of person.

A person who can love beyond convenience.

A person who can sacrifice without immediate reward.

A person who can tell the truth when lying would be easier.

A person who can forgive when resentment would feel more satisfying.

A person who can possess power without becoming possessed by it.

A person who can receive success without making success his identity.

A person who can suffer without allowing suffering to determine his character.

You can reject the metaphysical claims of Christianity and still recognise the philosophical seriousness of that project.

The Uncomfortable Part

In fact, this is where I think the “Christians are delusional” argument becomes uncomfortable.

Because if Christianity is merely a system designed to keep people afraid of hell, then the Christian life would be a strange way of constructing it.

Its central moral figure tells people to love their enemies.

Its central ethic repeatedly directs attention toward people who cannot repay you.

Its spiritual disciplines require self-examination.

Its conception of greatness is tied to service.

Its vision of leadership is inseparable from responsibility.

Its treatment of wealth contains repeated warnings about what wealth can do to the human heart.

Its conception of holiness reaches into places where external applause cannot reach.

There is something intellectually interesting about a worldview that asks:

What kind of person are you becoming?

And I think this is where we need to distinguish between belief and fruit.

A Christian can believe the wrong things.

A Christian can behave terribly.

Christian history contains enough failures, abuses and contradictions to make that obvious.

But the failures of Christians do not automatically settle the question of whether the Christian ideal itself is defective.

In fact, some of the most profound Christian traditions of charity, hospitality, education, medicine, care for the vulnerable and sacrificial service have emerged from the conviction that human beings possess dignity because they are made in the image of God.

The Christian story has repeatedly produced people who gave their lives to people who could give them nothing in return.

That does not prove Christianity true.

But it does complicate the claim that Christianity is simply an elaborate mechanism for personal comfort.

What About Upbringing?

There is another philosophical problem with reducing faith to upbringing.

Suppose I inherited Christianity from my parents.

So what?

I inherited language too.

I inherited a culture.

I inherited assumptions about morality, relationships, and human dignity.

Inheritance explains where a belief came from.

It does not establish whether the belief is true or even false.

A proposition does not become false because someone inherited it.

Neither does it become true because someone inherited it.

It still has to be examined.

Where a belief came from and whether the belief is true are two different questions.

That distinction matters.

Principles, Precepts, Patterns

This is where I have become increasingly interested in Christianity as a system of principles, precepts and patterns.

The principles tell me something about reality.

The precepts tell me how to live within that reality.

The patterns reveal what happens when these things are repeatedly practised.

And when I look at the Christian life through that lens, I find something worth taking seriously.

The Christian life contains a coherent philosophy of human formation.

It is concerned with the mind.

The body.

Desire.

Character.

Community.

Work.

Relationships.

Suffering.

Death.

Meaning.

Eternity.

It is attempting to answer a much larger question than:

“How do I get to heaven?”

It is also asking:

“What kind of human being should I become while I am here?”

The Question Beneath the Question

And perhaps that is why I find the Christian life compelling.

If Christianity is true, then everything I have lived for has an eternal horizon.

If Christianity were false, I would still have spent my life trying to become the kind of man I believe humanity ought to become.

That is not a complete argument for Christianity.

I am not pretending it is.

Truth cannot be established merely by asking whether a worldview produces a pleasant life.

But it does challenge a particular caricature.

The Christian is not necessarily living this way because he is terrified of what happens after death.

He may be living this way because he has become convinced that:

This is what human beings are for.

And if that conviction is true, then Christianity offers more than survival after death.

It offers a vision of human flourishing that begins here and extends beyond here.

So, Are Christians Delusional?

Maybe.

But before we dismiss the delusion, perhaps we should examine the kind of human being it is trying to produce.

Because if the Christian life makes you more capable of love, more disciplined in desire, more generous with what you possess, more willing to forgive, more attentive to the dignity of another person, more responsible with power, more courageous in suffering, and more conscious of the eternal significance of your choices, then even the hypothetical atheist observer has a philosophical question to answer:

What exactly is so obviously irrational about wanting to become that kind of person?

~ Ezra Anya

If this thought made you pause, I would love to hear what you think. Especially if you disagree.
