posts.title: You Cannot Live a Perfect Life
posts.content:
Recently, my colleagues hosted a party for me to mark a significant moment in my career journey.

At some point, they were asked to share their thoughts about me and my work.

One particular comment stayed with me.

Someone said,

“Ezra would always give not just his 100% to his job, but 120%, and still come back and find flaws in it and fix it.”

I laughed when I heard it.

Then I thought about it.

Because that sentence probably captures one of the most defining parts of my personality.

I have always been a perfectionist.

I guess I still am.

Perhaps that is one of the first things I have had to learn about perfectionism. You never quite arrive at a place where you can declare yourself “cured”.

You remain in recovery.

I still think there is something strangely seductive about perfectionism, though.

It often looks like discipline.

It can look like conscientiousness, meticulousness, attention to detail, high standards, and an almost obsessive commitment to doing things properly.

These qualities have helped me produce good work; I won’t lie.

They can make you careful with your words, thoughtful about your decisions, and sensitive to details that other people overlook.

I have benefited from those parts of my personality.

However, I have also paid dearly for them.

There is a point at which a strength becomes maladaptive. The same attention to detail that helps you produce excellent work can become an inability to tolerate others. The same desire to make good decisions can become paralysis. I have experienced this in opportunities, my faith, and even in romantic relationships.

For me, perfectionism has had a psychological dimension that I am still learning to understand.

It eventually translated to OCD, specifically what I found out to be Just Right OCD. I have not spoken much about this publicly.

Perhaps I have been waiting for the right time. Perhaps the perfectionist in me has been waiting for the right way and right moment to explain something difficult to explain even to yourself. Maybe I will talk about it properly someday.

What I can say now is that when I began to calculate the cost of perfectionism in my own life, I realised something uncomfortable.

It was costing me more than it was giving me.

It cost me time.

It cost me energy, both mental and physical.

It cost me opportunities because I was constantly preparing, constantly learning, constantly refining, while rarely feeling ready.

And perhaps the most expensive cost has been relationships.

I once lost a very precious protegee because of my extreme expectations of him. Looking back now, I can recognise how disproportionate some of those expectations were.

At the time, though, they felt reasonable.

I was simply expecting from him what I expected from myself.

That was the problem.

I had mistaken the standards I imposed upon myself for a universal measure of how another person should function.

Perfectionism can do that to you.

It can turn your internal standard into an invisible law and then make you frustrated when other human beings fail to live according to it.

I have spent a considerable amount of time unlearning this.

So these are five lessons I am learning as a recovering perfectionist.

1. Let the past remain in the past. Let go

I am learning to stop revisiting old versions of myself.

There is a peculiar form of psychological bondage that comes from constantly auditing your past.

You replay the decision.

You reconstruct the conversation.

You imagine the version of yourself who should have known better.

You calculate what you lost because of one mistake and then spend years trying to emotionally recover the life that might have existed had you chosen differently.

Perfectionism makes this particularly difficult because it carries an implicit belief that if you analyse something long enough, you can eventually arrive at the perfect understanding of it.

You cannot.

Some things are simply over.

You made mistakes.

You will make more. Trust me,

There are things you will understand in five years that you do not understand today. There are decisions you will make today that your future self will find difficult to defend.

That is part of being human.

Progress is not measured by the absence of mistakes. It is measured by your capacity to metabolise experience.

You make the mistake.

You extract the lesson.

You integrate what happened into your understanding of yourself.

Then you continue living.

There is a difference between learning from the past and remaining psychologically attached to it.

Reflection can produce wisdom. Rumination can produce exhaustion.

I have had to learn that revisiting an old wound repeatedly does not make me wiser. Sometimes it simply keeps the wound psychologically active and alive.

There are things I would do differently.

I have accepted that.

I am learning to let that be enough.

2. You do not need external validation to do excellent work

One of the strange things about perfectionism is that the desire to do things well can gradually become entangled with the desire to be seen doing things well.

Read it again.

That creates a problem.

People are inconsistent. Their attention fluctuates. Their standards change.

Their appreciation is affected by mood, context, familiarity, and a hundred other variables you cannot control.

When your internal standard depends on external feedback, your emotional state becomes tethered to something inherently unstable.

Someone praises you, you feel competent.

Someone ignores you, you question yourself.

Someone critiques you, you begin wondering whether everything you have done is inadequate.

That is exhausting.

I am honestly learning to build a more internal locus of evaluation.

There are things I should do well because they deserve to be done well.

There are things I should finish because they need to be finished.

There are promises I should keep because I made them.

The quality of my work should have an internal logic.

My motivation cannot always depend on applause.

This has also changed the way I think about excellence.

Excellence is not the same thing as performance for an audience.

Sometimes nobody notices.

Sometimes the reward is simply knowing that you gave the work the attention it deserved. You gave it your best.

There is a quiet dignity in that.

When your standard becomes internally anchored, you become less psychologically vulnerable to fluctuations in recognition.

You can receive praise without becoming dependent on it.

You can receive criticism without allowing it to dismantle your sense of self.

You can keep doing good work in rooms where nobody is clapping.

And I think that is a healthier form of excellence.

3. Every choice comes with its own regret

Perfectionists often want the perfect decision.

The perfectly researched decision.

The decision with the least uncertainty.

The option that gives you the highest probability of success and the lowest probability of regret. Lol.

Life does not offer that kind of transaction.

Every meaningful decision closes some doors.

Even good decisions carry loss.

Choose one career, and you abandon another possible life.

Commit to one person and a thousand hypothetical possibilities disappear.

Move to one city, and you stop living in the places you could have chosen.

Say yes to one thing and your yes quietly becomes a no to something else.

There is always an opportunity cost.

I have started thinking differently about regret because of this.

Perhaps the better question is not, “Which decision guarantees that I will never regret this?”

Perhaps the question is, “Which regret am I willing to carry?”

That question feels more honest.

You cannot optimise your way out of regret.

You can only decide what kind of regret you are willing to live with.

Every path extracts a psychological cost.

That has helped me make decisions with greater equanimity.

I do not need every decision to feel perfect.

I need to know that I can live with what the decision requires of me.

4. To become someone you have never been, you must do what you have never done

This one sounds obvious until you realise how much of personal growth is an encounter with unfamiliarity.

We often want transformation while preserving the conditions that produced our current selves.

We want a different life while maintaining the same routines.

We want greater courage while avoiding situations that make us afraid.

We want deeper relationships while remaining emotionally guarded.

We want new opportunities while still waiting until we feel completely prepared.

Familiarity offers psychological comfort.

The brain prefers predictability. Familiar patterns require less cognitive effort. They give us a sense of control.

However, growth interferes with that arrangement.

At some point, you have to become a beginner again.

You have to tolerate incompetence.

You have to be seen trying something you are not yet good at.

You have to make decisions before you possess complete information.

You have to endure the discomfort of being temporarily inadequate at something you desperately want to become good at.

This has been particularly difficult for me because perfectionism wants excellence before exposure.

Life rarely works in that order.

You become through doing.

You become more articulate by speaking.

You become better at relationships by relating.

You become more disciplined by repeatedly keeping difficult commitments.

There is a version of yourself that exists on the other side of experiences you have never permitted yourself to have.

You cannot think your way into becoming that person.

At some point, you have to act. And act embarrassingly.

5. Certainty is a myth

This may be the most difficult lesson for me.

I like certainty.

I like to know.

I like to understand. I like to have a robust, comprehensive explanation for everything.

I like to have enough information to feel that I have accounted for the variables and arrived at the most defensible conclusion.

Perfectionism loves certainty because certainty feels like control.

You think that if you can know enough, prepare enough, analyse enough, and anticipate enough, you can protect yourself from making the wrong move.

But human life is characterised by irreducible uncertainty.

You cannot know how a relationship will unfold.

You cannot know whether an opportunity will work.

You cannot know exactly who you will become.

You cannot know whether the decision you made at twenty-five will still make sense at thirty-five.

You cannot even know with absolute certainty how you will feel about the things you are presently convinced you want.

At some point, every person has to make peace with epistemic limitation.

There are things you simply cannot know yet.

There are things you may never know.

That does not mean you stop thinking carefully.

It means you stop demanding omniscience from yourself.

I am learning to make decisions with the information I have.

I am learning to leave room for revision.

I am learning that uncertainty does not automatically mean danger. Sometimes it is simply uncertainty.

And perhaps this is what recovery from perfectionism has increasingly looked like for me.

Allowing things to be unfinished.

Allowing myself to be imperfect.

Allowing other people to be human.

Allowing decisions to carry uncertainty.

Allowing the future to remain partially obscured.

Allowing myself to move before I feel completely ready.

I still struggle with this. I won’t lie.

I still catch myself overthinking.

I still want things to feel right.

I still find myself refining something already good enough to be released.

The difference is that I am becoming more conscious of it.

And perhaps that is what recovery means.

You notice the pattern earlier. You interrupt it sooner.

You return to a healthier way of thinking.

Then you do it again.

That has changed more than the way I work.

It has changed the way I think about myself.

I am beginning to understand that a meaningful life requires a certain tolerance for imperfection.

There will always be something to improve.

There will always be something you could have done differently.

At some point, you have to stop treating your incompleteness as evidence that you are failing.

You are becoming.

And trust me, you can be a masterpiece and a work in progress at the same time.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: Stop Pursuing Your Losses
posts.content:
Sometimes, the reason we are not making progress is that we are still trying to recover something we lost in the past.

We are pursuing our losses.

In investing, there is a principle that warns against chasing losses.

After a bad decision, the desire to recover what was lost can influence the next decision. You begin to act from the weight of what happened rather than the wisdom required for what comes next.

I have wondered if we approach life in the same way.

Perhaps some of us are still trying to compensate for mistakes we made years, months, weeks ago.

You made a mistake, and now you are carrying the pressure to prove that you are better than that mistake.

You spent years in a relationship that did not end the way you hoped. Now you are trying to recover the time you believe you lost.

You have not prayed consistently. You look at the days you missed and feel the need to make up for all of them before you can return.

But the past does not always need repayment.

Sometimes, it needs understanding.

There are lessons hidden inside our losses. Some experiences reveal patterns we had ignored. Others expose the places where we lacked wisdom, discipline, courage, or discernment.

Learn from them.

Then move.

You cannot return to yesterday and make a different decision.

You can carry what yesterday taught you into the life ahead.

The relationship ended.

Take the wisdom with you.

You missed the days.

Pray today.

You made the mistake.

Learn what it revealed, then allow yourself to grow beyond it.

I think many people delay their future because they are still negotiating with their past.

They keep revisiting the loss.

They keep calculating what it cost.

They keep searching for a way to recover every moment.

Meanwhile, life continues to move.

There is a point where reflection must become direction.

You have looked back long enough to understand what happened.

Now look ahead and decide what you will do with what you have learned.

The words of Scripture come to mind:

“Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on...”

Forgetting does not always mean losing the memory.

Sometimes, it means refusing to let the memory determine your next step.

The past can teach you without becoming the place where you remain.

So, as we enter a new month, perhaps you do not need to recover everything you lost.

Perhaps you need to release the pressure of recovery.

Perhaps you need to stop trying to make up for every missed opportunity and begin paying attention to the opportunity in front of you.

There is still time.

There is still purpose.

There is still something ahead that deserves your full attention.

Learn from what is behind.

Then press toward what lies ahead.

I am rooting for you.

P.S. I am certain you are happy to hear from me again. See you soon.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: Is Christianity Really “Not a Religion”?
posts.content:
There are certain things you will never hear the early Church Fathers say.

There are modern, popular Christian slogans that, if uttered in the presence of Thomas Aquinas, Irenaeus, or Justin Martyr, would have been met with absolute bewilderment—and perhaps a polite scoff.

Today, I want to examine one of the most famous that has been on my mind for a couple of months:

“Christianity is not a religion—it is a relationship.”

Whenever I look at a theological discourse, in my bid to be intellectually honest and rigorous, I do two things:

First, I apply first-principles thinking to the concept being examined.

Second, I deliberately develop the strongest possible case for the varying views associated with that concept (often called “steel-manning”).

I do this while working to limit my personal bias to the barest minimum. I know that complete objectivity might be an illusion, but intellectual honesty is a discipline I seek to practice.

So, when we confidently declare from pulpits and on social media that Christianity is not a religion, we must pause and ask: Sincerely, what do we actually mean?

Let us stress-test this properly.

The Charitable View: The Pastoral Intent

Let me begin by developing the strongest case for this statement.

The instinct to push back against “religion” is often a good one.

When proponents say Christianity is not a religion, they are trying to make a deeply meaningful distinction. They are arguing that Christianity is not primarily about ritual compliance, moral performance, or mere institutional belonging. It is about a personal, transformative union with a living God.

The intent here is highly pastoral and fiercely evangelistic.
It is a necessary pushback against dead formalism.

There is a very real theological nerve being touched here:

  • Christological: Jesus’s constant confrontation with the empty, hypocritical religiosity of the Pharisees.

  • Pauline: Paul’s aggressive polemic against the “works of the law” in Galatians.

  • Historical: The Reformation’s rallying cry of Sola Fide (Faith Alone) by Martin Luther and his fellow protestants.

These all point toward a profound, undeniable truth: The core of Christianity is not achieved through performance and grit; it is received through partnership and grace.

Where the Statement Breaks Down

However, while the sentiment is beautiful, the phrasing is fundamentally flawed. When subjected to theological, historical, and logical scrutiny, the claim that “Christianity is not a religion” quickly collapses.

Personally, here are five reasons why:

1. It is Definitionally False

By every lexical and sociological definition available, Christianity is a religion. It has established doctrine, corporate liturgy, sacred texts, communal worship, ethical codes, rites of initiation (like baptism), and institutional structures. Denying this does not make it profoundly spiritual; it simply makes it sound like we have not read a dictionary.

2. The Bible Does Not Avoid the Word

If God hated the concept of religion, the writers of Scripture would have discarded it. Yet, James 1:27 clearly states:

“Pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their trouble, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world.”

James does not reject the concept of religion; he redefines it. He recalibrates it around authentic transformation rather than empty ritual. That is a vastly different intellectual move.

3. “Relationship” Requires Structure

If we claim Christianity is strictly a “relationship,” we must realize that all healthy relationships have boundaries, expectations, and patterns.

At a communal level, these patterns are exactly what religion describes. You cannot claim to have a deeply intimate relationship with God and then act as though the gathering of the brethren, the administration of the sacraments, and the public reading of Scripture are optional add-ons.

Every relationship is sustained by the structure substantiating it.

4. It Creates a False, Dangerous Binary

Pitting “religion” against “relationship” is a false dichotomy that ignores the very nature of the Incarnation.

The Incarnation itself—the Word becoming flesh (John 1:14)—is God entering into form. It is the divine becoming embodied, particular, and historical. Therefore, Christianity is irreducibly relational and irreducibly structured.

Trying to escape the “religion” framework often produces untethered communities: churches with no accountability, no sound doctrine, and no historical liturgy. And historically, churches devoid of STRUCTURE and ROUTINE tend to go sideways very fast.

5. It is historically novel and culturally loaded.

We must realize that this phrasing is largely a 20th-century evangelical American invention. It is culturally loaded rhetoric.

It would have completely confused Augustine of Hippo, Thomas Aquinas, John Calvin, and the early Apologists. None of the great minds who defended our faith felt the need to apologize for it by saying, “Do not worry, we are not a religion.” They boldly defended the superiority and truth of the Christian religion against pagan alternatives.

Subscribe now

The Vulnerabilities of a “Religionless” Christianity

This is not merely a debate over semantics; this phrasing creates profound structural vulnerabilities within the Body of Christ. When we convince a generation that Christianity requires no “religion,” we unintentionally disarm them.

The Trap of Hyper-Individualism: If faith is only a relationship, it quickly devolves into a private, “Me and Jesus” echo chamber.

I have literally heard people say things like “I am the temple of God, hence I don’t need to go to church”

Religion demands community. It forces us into the pew next to people we do not naturally like, teaching us the crucible of long-suffering, submission, and grace. A religionless Christianity breeds isolated believers who consume sermons online but submit to no local authority or accountability.

Doctrinal Drift and Emotionalism: Relationships based entirely on feelings are dangerously volatile. Without the “religious” framework of historical creeds, rigorous theology, and sound apologetics, faith becomes purely subjective. We see and hear egregious things daily, and it is backed up with “The spirit told me:” and who are you to argue against the “spirit,” which is their emotions and desire?

When the emotional high fades, the foundation crumbles. This creates a vacuum where believers are tossed by every wind of doctrine, making them prime targets for manipulation, heresy, and deconstruction.

The Crisis of Generational Transmission: You cannot easily pass down a subjective emotional experience, but you can pass down a religion. The scaffolding of religion—catechism, liturgy, corporate sacraments, and sacred traditions—exists specifically to transmit the faith to the next generation. When we strip away the religion, we leave our children with a vague spiritual sentimentalism that lacks the fiber to withstand the intellectual hostility of a dark and progressively perverse world.

The Resolution: A Better Way Forward

The popular statement is trying to communicate something deeply true, but in a remarkably clumsy way.

If we want to capture the heartbeat of the Gospel without sacrificing our intellectual and theological integrity, a much better, solid formulation would be this:

“Christianity is not merely a religion—it is a covenant relationship that religion can only ever attempt to approximate.”

You may need to read it again.

To survive the complexities of our time, we must abandon this false binary once and for all. Christianity is a deeply intimate relationship just as much as it is a solid, structured religion.

You cannot separate the two if you intend to stand firm and fervent in a dark and untoward generation.

A relationship without the framework of religion is like a fire without a fireplace—it might burn hot for a moment, but it is ultimately untethered, vulnerable to the winds of culture, and quick to burn out. Conversely, religion without a relationship is just cold ash on a dead altar.

The structure is what sustains the fire. The ancient creeds, the communal accountability, the sacraments, and the liturgy are the robust religious wineskins designed to carry the new wine of the Holy Ghost.

When the intellectual and moral storms of this age hit, your subjective feelings will not anchor you; the historic, structured, and communal reality of the Christian faith will.

Let us not discard the structure in our pursuit of the Spirit.

We need both.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: He Was Delivered. He Was Raised.
posts.content:
A meditation on Romans 4:25 for Easter.

There is a verse that has sat with me for longer than I can fully account for. I always pause for some minutes whenever I come across it. And providentially I started studying the book this month.

I stay with with the verse not because it is obscure.

It is not. It sits quietly in the fourth chapter of Romans, tucked between arguments about faith and righteousness and the ancient story of a man called Abraham who believed God in the dark.

But the more I have sat with it, the more I have come to believe that Romans 4:25 is one of the most compressed and complete statements of the Gospel ever written.

He was delivered up for our offences and was raised again for our justification.

Twenty words. And inside those twenty words — the entire blueprint of what God has done for humanity.

I want to walk through this slowly. Because slow is the only speed that does this justice.

Walk with me…

He Was Delivered Up.

Notice the language first. Not — He died. Not — He was killed. He was delivered up.

The Greek word is paredothe — a word that carries the weight of intentional transfer. Of being handed over. Of a transaction completed by attention, not by accident.

This was not a tragedy that spun out of control. This was not Rome winning and heaven losing. This was the Father, in the most unfathomable act of love the universe has ever witnessed, delivering His own Son into the hands of suffering, of shame, of the sting of death — on our behalf.

Isaiah had seen it coming seven centuries earlier. He was wounded for our transgressions. He was bruised for our iniquities.

And Paul, writing to the Romans, returns to the same staggering truth. He was delivered up. Handed over. Given.

He was made a sacrifice. It happened by the Father's intention and the Son's submission.

For our offences.

Not His own. He had none. The sinless one, delivered up for the sinful ones. The righteous one, handed over for the unrighteous. The one in whom there was no darkness, submerged into the full weight of our darkness — so that our darkness could finally and fully be dealt with.

This is the cross.

Not a symbol. Not a metaphor. Not a story we tell to make ourselves feel better about the human condition.

A real man. Real scourge. Real nails. Real wood. Real death.

And behind all of it — real love. The kind that does not calculate the cost before it commits. The kind that looks at what it is walking into, doesn't look away but walks in anyway.

He was delivered up for our offences.

And Was Raised Again.

But the sentence does not end at the cross. It was never designed to.

The Gospel that stops at Good Friday is not yet the full Gospel. The cross without the resurrection is only half a sentence. Powerful, yes. Meaningful, yes. Perfect, no.

And so Paul writes — and was raised again.

The resurrection is not an afterthought. It is not a postscript added to make the story more pleasant. The resurrection is the vindication. The declaration. The evidence that the cross accomplished everything it was sent to accomplish.

When God raised Jesus from the dead, He was making a statement that has echoed through eternity.

The debt is paid. The sentence is complete. Death has no final claim here. Sin has no final word here. The grave could not hold what it was never meant to keep.

He has disarmed principalities and powers and made them a public spectacle.

He was raised.

For Our Justification.

And now we arrive at the most personal word in the verse.

Our.

This is not a theological abstraction. Not a historical event sealed off in the past with no reach into the present. Our justification. Mine. Yours. The person reading this at whatever hour, in whatever season, carrying whatever weight.

Justification is a legal term.

It means to be declared righteous. Not to be made slightly better. Not to be put on probation pending further review. To be declared — once, completely, finally — righteous before God.

This is what the resurrection secured.

The cross dealt with our sins. The resurrection secured our standing. Together they form the two expressions of the greatest act in human history — the removal of what was wrong and the establishment of what is right.

He was delivered up — so that our offences could be carried away.

He was raised — so that our justification could be declared complete.

This is not just religion.

Religion is humanity's attempt to close the gap between itself and God through effort, through ritual, through the accumulation of enough good to outweigh the bad.

This is the Gospel. The Gospel is God closing the gap Himself. At infinite personal cost. With no assistance required and no contribution accepted.

Read that again.

He did it. Completely. Finally. For us.

A Thought For This Easter.

I have been thinking about what it means to truly believe this. Not to know it intellectually — many people know it intellectually. But to believe it in the way that changes the texture of how you think, see yourself and ultimately how you live.

To wake up in the morning and know that you are not under condemnation. Not because you have been good enough. But because He was delivered up and He was raised and the verdict of justification has already been declared over your life.

To walk into difficulty and know that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the same God who is present in your current situation. That resurrection is not just a historical event. It is the operating principle of the Christian life.

God brings life out of death. He always has. He always will.

To hold your failures — and we all have them — without the crushing weight of guilt that has nowhere to go. Because your offences were the very thing He was delivered up for. They are not a surprise to Him. They were the whole point of the cross.

This Easter, I want to invite you to do something simple and profound.

Sit with Romans 4:25. Not as a verse to memorize. As a revelation to imbibe.

He was delivered up for your offences.

He was raised again for your justification.

Both halves are about you. Both halves are for you. Both halves are already complete, finished and perfected.

You do not have to earn what has already been given. You do not have to secure what has already been settled. You do not have to prove what has already been declared.

You are justified.

Because He was delivered. And because He was raised.

Happy Easter.

Romans 4:25 — He was delivered up for our offences and was raised again for our justification.

This is my first piece back on Substack after a season of building quietly. I have missed writing here. There is something about long form that the short form world cannot replace — the ability to go deep, to stay with a thought long enough to feel it move something. That is what this space is for. I am glad to be back. And I am glad you are here.

If this piece found you at the right time, share it with someone who needs it today.

And subscribe if you want to stay in the room for what is coming next.

~ Ezra Anya

posts.title: The "New Year, New Me" Fallacy
posts.content:
Hey there,

It has been three months since I last sent a letter to this inbox.

In the digital world, three months is an eternity. It is enough time to be forgotten by the algorithms and buried by the noise. But I have always believed that deep work requires deep silence.

If you have been wondering where I went, I want to assure you: I did not disappear.
I was simply mining.

I have a philosophy that you cannot feed others if your own pot is empty.
So, I took a season to retreat, to research, and to build.

I stepped back to do the boring, rigorous work of thinking, researching, and writing.
I wanted to understand a specific problem that plagues almost everyone I know—including myself—at this time of year.

The Annual Lie.

We are approaching the end of the year. You can feel it in the air. The panic of unmet goals is setting in. The anxiety of “what did I actually achieve?” is rising. And right on cue, the comforting lie begins to whisper:

“Don’t worry. Next year will be different. January 1st is a fresh start.”

I am writing this letter to tell you one thing: Do not listen to that voice.

Waiting for January 1st is a trap.

The calendar changes automatically, but your mind does not. If you try to build a new life on an old foundation simply because the date changed, you are guaranteed to collapse by February.

I realized that we don’t need more motivation. We have plenty of desire. What we lack is a System.

So, during my silence, I wrote a book about it.

It is called RESOLVE: Why Waiting Until January is a Trap.

This is not a collection of motivational quotes. It is a tactical manual on how to hack your brain, build systems, and actually change your life.

I poured my background in research, my theological convictions, and my obsession with human psychology into these pages.

Inside, I break down:

  • The Protocol: How to brutally audit your life so you stop repeating the same mistakes.

  • The Neuroscience: How to hack your Reticular Activating System (RAS) to spot opportunities you are currently missing.

  • The Strategy: Why you must “pre-load” your habits now (in November/December) to avoid the January crash.

  • The Psychology: How to overcome the fear of your own brilliance (The Jonah Complex).

I wrote this for you. I wrote this so we don’t have to have the same conversation about “doing better” next year.

If you are tired of the cycle of hope followed by disappointment, this book is your exit strategy.

You can get your copy here: https://selar.com/ru416n406c

Buy Resolve Book

Do not wait for the New Year. The magic isn’t in the date; it’s in the resolve.

The best time to start was yesterday. The second-best time is now.
Start now.

I missed you all. It feels good to be back.

In pursuit of a life by design, not by default.

~ Ezra Anya
